items.title: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants
items.summary: The South African Supreme Court of Appeal recently dismissed the government’s appeal against a ruling that struck down plans for 1,500 megawatts of new coal-fired power. The so-called #CancelCoal case was brought by a coalition of environmental NGOs that argued the new planned coal capacity violates children’s constitutional rights to a healthy environment. Already, air pollution from coal-fired power plants kills more than 2,200 South Africans each year and “causes thousands of cases of bronchitis and asthma,” according to a statement from the Centre for Environmental Rights. The Minister of Electricity and Energy argued that additional coal capacity is necessary for energy security. A previous High Court judgment ruled against the plan “on the basis that it violates the right to an environment not harmful to health and well-being,” per the statement. “The High Court further found that government’s arguments about grid stability offered by coal, was not sufficient justification for the violation of constitutional rights,” said Michelle Sithole in an email to Mongabay. Sithole is senior associate in the pollution and climate change program at the Centre for Environmental Rights, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the court case. The Minister appealed the High Court decision. The recent Court of Appeal’s decision dismissed the Minister’s appeal, meaning the previous High Court decision stands. “While this does not mean a definitive end to the development of new coal-fired power as part of the energy security policy, it does mean that government has a higher…
items.t: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants

items.title: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
items.summary: Deforestation, organized crime and the expansion of cattle ranching have led the government in Honduras to announce an “environmental emergency” in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, the largest protected area in the country. The 36-month emergency, issued as a presidential decree on Nov. 10, will devote 1.5 billion Honduran lempiras (more than $55 million) over the next three years to halt “environmental deterioration,” according to an official statement. “The initiative represents a commitment by the government to move from addressing threats to sustained intervention, with defined resources and institutional responsibilities,” presidential legal advisor Roberto Zacapa said in the statement. The more than 832,000-hectare (2 million-acre) reserve stretches across the departments of Gracias a Dios, Colón and Olancho, and includes numerous Indigenous Miskito, Pech and Garífuna communities. In 1982, a section of it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The reserve’s remote location along the Nicaraguan border has made it vulnerable to deforestation, drug trafficking, cattle ranching, gold mining, wildlife trafficking, roadbuilding and other illegal activities. At least 6,691 hectares (16,533 acres) of forest were cut down between 2023 and 2025, according to the Forest Conservation Institute (ICF), the agency managing the country’s forests. Since 2011, the reserve has been on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage in Danger, a list of sites facing serious threats to their environmental or cultural heritage. “It’s like the wild west, where there’s no law and people come in…
items.t: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve

items.title: Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable | Letters
items.summary:
Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory

I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World (‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November).

To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally.

items.title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
items.summary: A record number of wildfires burned more than 14,062 square miles in the U.S. this year, leaving behind charred trees and scorched vegetation. But less-obvious are the impacts they had on the streams and rivers that provide drinking water to urban and rural communities across the country. After a wildfire burns a watershed, rain will carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities. Utilities must turn off the intake to keep the sediment-filled water from contaminating their systems and switch to another source, if it’s available. New studies found that wildfires can contaminate water for up to 15 years. These findings are especially concerning as climate change has led to an increase in the number and size of wildfires in the U.S. By Martha Bellisele, Associated Press Banner image: A helicopter drops water on the Grizzly Creek Fire on the east end of Glenwood Canyon, Aug. 17, 2020 near Glenwood Springs, Colo. Image courtesy of Helen H. Richardson/The Denver Post via Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US

items.title: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)
items.summary: Leading a group of ecology students down a trail through the forest behind Merrimack College, in North Andover, Massachusetts, U.S., where I teach biology part-time as an adjunct professor, I spot a garter snake. As it rapidly starts crawling away, I grab the snake by its tail. Excited students gather round to check out the foot-long striped serpent, while taking photos with their cell phones. I tell them a bit about garter snakes and ask if anyone wants to hold it. “I do!” one of the students says. I gently hand her the snake. “That’s really cool. I’ve never held a snake before,” she says, before handing it to another eager student. Then we turn the snake loose and continue on our way. Merrimack College biology students with a garter snake found during an ecology lab on campus, North Andover, MA, September 2025. Image courtesy of Don Lyman. Since I began at Merrimack in 1997, I’ve taught mainly ecology labs. Most of the ecology lab sessions are outdoors, so they’re like weekly field trips. They give students the opportunity to step outside of laboratories and classrooms and interact with nature. Field courses provide the same opportunity for teachers. When I head off into the woods with students in tow, I’m in my element. Whether I’m diving into the bushes and scrambling on my hands and knees to catch a snake or a frog to show the class, pointing out a hawk circling overhead, or teaching students how to identify various…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)

items.title: Mongabay shark meat investigation shortlisted for two journalism awards in Brazil
items.summary: A Mongabay investigation that revealed large-scale government purchases of shark meat for schools, hospitals, prisons and other public institutions in Brazil has been named as a finalist for two Brazilian journalism awards               . Published in 2025 in collaboration with the Pulitzer Center, the investigation tracked 1,012 public procurements issued since 2004 to purchase more than 5,400 metric tons of shark meat, worth at least 112 million reais ($20.1 million). The findings sparked environmental and public health concerns. Sharks, some of them endangered, accumulate heavy metals such as mercury and arsenic in their tissues. High levels of these contaminants can pose health risks, particularly for children. Mongabay’s reporting is one of three finalists for the Cláudio Weber Abramo Data Journalism Award in the investigation category, which recognizes “work of high social impact that applies data analysis to shed light on topics of public interest.” The series is also one of 25 finalists for the Mosca Award, which honors investigative reporting and projects focused on transparency, access to public information and open data. Senior editor Philip Jacobson and investigative reporters Karla Mendes and Fernanda Wenzel reported the series for Mongabay, working with Kuang Keng Kuek Ser, then data editor at the Pulitzer Center. The investigation has had widespread impact, prompting a request for a public hearing in Brazil’s lower house of Congress and stirring debate in the fishing industry over the risks of eating shark meat. Shark meat was banned in 1,200 schools run by…
items.t: Mongabay shark meat investigation shortlisted for two journalism awards in Brazil

items.title: Fruit bats emerge as unlikely allies in the Atlantic Forest restoration
items.summary: Bats have long occupied a sinister place in Western pop culture. Ever since Bram Stoker published Dracula in 1897, these nocturnal mammals have been associated with vampires. Outside fiction, however, only three of the world’s roughly 1,500 known bat species feed on blood — and only one targets mammals such as cattle and other livestock. Even then, humans are rarely on the menu. Bats represent the second most diverse group of mammals, behind rodents. They also provide essential ecosystem services, including insect pest control, pollination and seed dispersal; around a third of all species feed on fruit or nectar. A fruit-eating bat won over Lays Cherobim Parolin early in her career. As she was about to graduate with a degree in biology, the scientist wanted to work with larger mammals but ended up joining a bat research project instead. The first time she held one, as she removed it from a mist net, she was hooked. “People have no idea that bats are seed dispersers and have the potential to restore [natural] areas. They never remember them, they only remember birds,” Parolin, now a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná (PUC), said. Researcher Lays Cherobim Parolin sets up an experimental structure with essential oils to attract bats. Image courtesy of Gledson Vigiano Bianconi. The encounter left such an impression that Parolin got a tattoo on her arm of the great fruit-eating bat (Artibeus lituratus), a species identifiable by two pale stripes across its head. The tattoo serves as…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Fruit bats emerge as unlikely allies in the Atlantic Forest restoration

items.title: El Niño drove drought, but climate change intensified Indonesia’s fire crisis: Study
items.summary: Human-caused climate change significantly amplified extreme heat during Indonesia’s 2026 fire season, turning an El Niño-driven drought into a severe regional crisis, according to a recent rapid analysis. The report was released by World Weather Attribution (WWA), a global network of researchers who analyze the influence of climate change in extreme weather events. The researchers analyzed weather conditions across western Indonesia during the dry season between August and October 2026, when fires burned approximately 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) of peatland and rainforest. The resulting toxic haze exposed 12.5 million people across Southeast Asia to hazardous air pollution and caused more than 400,000 respiratory infections in Indonesia alone, according to findings from the WWA report. Researchers found that while a strong El Niño was the primary driver of an “extreme lack of rainfall,” cutting seasonal precipitation by roughly 50% during the three months, record-breaking temperatures were overwhelmingly driven by global warming. Human-induced climate change made the season 1.6° Celsius (2.9° Fahrenheit) hotter; such extreme heat would be virtually impossible without greenhouse gas emissions, the researchers found. Meanwhile, El Niño added 0.3°C (0.5°F) of warming. Climate change also tripled the likelihood of weeklong hot, dry atmospheric extremes. “The top line of the study is that this year’s El Niño set the conditions for very low rainfall, a major fire season drought, and that this drought was then exacerbated by record heat throughout the fire season,…
items.t: El Niño drove drought, but climate change intensified Indonesia’s fire crisis: Study

items.title: ‘Incredibly unusual’ bird migrating from Siberia found in Cumbria – killed by cat
items.summary:
Siberian rubythroat was thousands of miles off course from its route to winter in south or south-east Asia

A bird that flies south from its breeding grounds in Siberia to winter in south and south-east Asia has been found thousands of miles off course in Cumbria. Regrettably, it was found by a cat.

Chris Hind, Cumbria’s county recorder for birds, said it was “extraordinary” that a Siberian rubythroat was found on his patch, albeit dead. There have been only 17 recorded instances of the bird in the UK, 15 of those in the northern Scottish isles.

items.title: Animal cafes and exotic pet trade bring wildlife disease risks into public spaces
items.summary: Mumbai-based veterinarian Rina Dev was hospitalized for four days recently with a lung infection. “I hope it’s not something from the parrots I was treating,” she told Mongabay India after being discharged from the hospital. Dev is an avian and exotic animal veterinarian who works closely with the forest department to treat animals that officials have seized from the illegal wildlife trade. Her concerns were valid. Psittacosis, caused by a bacterium, commonly infects people who handle birds, earning its nickname as “the bird handler’s disease.” A 2024 case describes a man who developed a high fever, chills, shortness of breath, cough, joint pain, and other symptoms — and broad-spectrum antibiotics didn’t help. He’d caught psittacosis from a parrot. With appropriate treatment, he recovered. There are many documented cases linking wildlife trade to human infections. In one instance, 15 customs officers in Belgium contracted psittacosis after being exposed to infected parakeets. A comprehensive review of the disease by the ICAR–Indian Veterinary Research Institute in 2021 noted it had “critical zoonotic potential.” But it’s just one of many pathogens that can cross the species barrier, sometimes adapting to new hosts in the process.  For decades, scientists have tried to inform the public that wildlife trade brings different species into unnatural proximity, creating opportunities for diseases to spread to animals that have no immunity to them. A 2026 report by Humane World for Animals warns that, in India, the exotic pet trade creates conditions that are extremely conducive…
items.t: Animal cafes and exotic pet trade bring wildlife disease risks into public spaces

items.title: A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’
items.summary:
Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing

On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.

A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

items.title: In India, volunteers map riverside trees to make a case for urban conservation
items.summary: Every weekend, several residents of Pune in India set out to map trees along the city’s riverbanks. It’s not just a weekend hobby; it’s meant to serve as evidence to protect the city’s greenery when developmental projects come up in the area, reports contributor Stephin Thomas for Mongabay. The volunteers are from Pune River Revival, a grassroots movement that formed in response to the Pune Riverfront Development Project, which aims to create promenades, recreational spaces, and infrastructure along the Mula and Mutha rivers. The project is estimated to cost around 47 billion rupees (about $500 million). “Personally, I want to protect the environment, but without this data, we cannot even grasp how much damage has already occurred,” Raghunandan Patil, a volunteer with the group, told Mongabay. “So to any nature lover, this gives an idea on what’s left to be saved. Apart from this, tree mapping provides evidence to present to the government or authorities when advocating for sustainable alternatives.” Patil said the group had been manually mapping the trees for a while, but began doing so more systematically in 2024 using the citizen-science app iNaturalist. The app allows all the data to be easily accessible and documented in specific projects. Such detailed documentation has already helped the group highlight the importance of some areas, such as the Ram-Mula Devrai, a sacred grove located at the confluence of the Ram and Mula rivers. This small forest patch is said by local communities to be the home of a village deity.…This article was originally published on…
items.t: In India, volunteers map riverside trees to make a case for urban conservation

items.title: This Animal Clinic Discovered Four Kittens Abandoned Inside A Box Outside Their Office And Helped Them Get Adopted
items.summary:
Finding a box of potato chips outside your workplace usually just means a quick trip to the garbage disposal. But when staff at the Blue Cross animal hospital in Hammersmith, London, arrived for work one morning, they discovered something rather unexpected inside such a box: four tiny kittens who had been abandoned and left to fend for themselves.

Fortunately, the little ones had ended up in the right place. The veterinary team quickly took them in, checked their health, and made sure they received the care they needed. And although their lives had gotten off to a rather unfortunate start, things were about to take a much happier turn. You might remember Blue Cross from our recent story about Bowie, the pony who grew up surrounded by cows. The UK animal welfare charity helps thousands of animals through its veterinary services, rescue efforts, and rehoming centers, giving pets in difficult circumstances another chance at a happy life.

Scroll down to see how the kittens are doing now and read the rest of the story.

The charity believes the ongoing cost-of-living crisis may be contributing, with some owners avoiding neutering their pets because of veterinary expenses. There are also concerns about people breeding cats to sell their kittens, only to struggle to find buyers and ultimately surrender or abandon the animals. “We’re so happy we managed to help these kittens into loving homes so quickly, and in time for Christmas,” Amanda Rumball, Veterinary Welfare Officer at Blue Cross, shared.

“We are urging anyone who is struggling to care for any…
items.t: This Animal Clinic Discovered Four Kittens Abandoned Inside A Box Outside Their Office And Helped Them Get Adopted

items.title: As incidents spike, Sri Lanka identifies 17 tuskers considered at high risk
items.summary: COLOMBO – Following widespread public outrage over the recent death of Kavantissa, one of Sri Lanka’s most celebrated wild tuskers, the government has decided to involve the country’s armed forces to protect vulnerable elephants, including some of the island’s remaining tuskers. The initiative, a coordinated operation involving Sri Lanka’s army, navy, air force and the Department of Wildlife Conservation, will have a dedicated operations center at the military headquarters to coordinate surveillance, information-sharing and responses to threats against elephants. Code named ‘Hasthi Sena’ in Sinhala, loosely translating to ‘an elephant army’ in English, the initiative aims to prevent elephant killings and curb wildlife crimes, strengthen intelligence gathering and support joint operations in areas affected by human-elephant conflict (HEC). The task force began its operations with raids last week across several areas, arresting several individuals involved in illegal activities including setting up trap guns or wire snares and possessing explosive-laden bait. The government took this measure amid renewed concern about the vulnerability of Sri Lanka’s remaining tuskers, particularly following the shooting and subsequent death of Kavantissa last month. While conservationists have welcomed greater institutional support for wildlife protection, they caution that the initiative must translate into a sustained conservation program rather than a temporary response to public pressure and not turn into yet another well-intentioned initiative that lost momentum after public attention…
items.t: As incidents spike, Sri Lanka identifies 17 tuskers considered at high risk

items.title: Country diary: Why did some trees fall in the storms and others not? It could be spalting | Kate Blincoe
items.summary:
Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: The woodland floor is littered with sycamore and ash, some revealing a pattern that runs through trunks like words in a stick of rock

An ash tree swayed, audibly groaning, a split in the trunk opening and closing like a mouth. Suffering from ash dieback, it seemed it could topple at any second here in the quiet of the woodland. A few weeks ago, Dad set the trail camera on it, to capture the moment of fall. Since then, two storms have churned through Norfolk – treating us gently compared with elsewhere, but nevertheless leaving casualties in their wake.

Fallen trunks now crisscross the woodland floor: sycamores, several ashes, an oak. But not the ash that had seemed so vulnerable. Why does one tree survive but another fall? I look closely at one of the ashes that succumbed to the winds, with its headless trunk jutting skyward, spiked and bare.

Continue reading...
items.t: Country diary: Why did some trees fall in the storms and others not? It could be spalting | Kate Blincoe

items.title: Can an ancient European forest be saved while securing Poland’s border?
items.summary: Straddling the border between Poland and Belarus, the ancient Białowieża Forest, one of Europe’s last remaining primeval woodlands, is already under stress from decades of drainage, drought and habitat fragmentation. As geopolitical tensions and security threats from Russia and Belarus rise, Poland plans to construct a massive network of military fortifications along its 700-kilometer (435-mile) eastern frontier through the “East Shield” initiative launched in 2024.  However, conservationists say the initiative, which would involve constructing traditional concrete bunkers, minefields and anti-tank ditches through the UNESCO World Heritage site, would cause severe destruction to local wildlife, reports contributor Marta Kasztelan for a Mongabay video. To prevent widespread habitat destruction, scientists from the Polish Academy of Sciences proposed an alternative strategy known as “warwilding” — restoring dense forests, rivers and bogs to serve as natural physical barriers against heavy military vehicles. “Places like this are very important because a tank can’t get through. So, if we expect an attack from that side, then we should preserve this type of environment,” Michal Zmihorski, a conservation biologist with the Polish Academy of Sciences, says in the video. To the researchers’ surprise, Poland’s military leadership embraced the proposal and incorporated ecological recovery into its border defense plans. “Our position is that the construction of the ‘East Shield’ and environmental protection can go hand in hand,” says Marek Pietrzak, a spokesperson for the Polish…
items.t: Can an ancient European forest be saved while securing Poland’s border?

items.title: In Brazil’s prey-rich Pantanal, jaguars reveal a surprisingly social side
items.summary: Jaguars are widely believed to be solitary cats, only tolerating others when mating or raising cubs. However, a new study in the Brazilian Pantanal has found the jaguars there often pair up and are far more social than expected. The Pantanal, the world’s largest wetland, has the world’s highest population density of jaguars (Panthera onca), where tourists are nearly guaranteed to spot them from a tour boat. This jaguar abundance has also attracted researchers. Since 2013, scientists with the Jaguar ID project have conducted daily surveys during the Pantanal’s dry season, June to October. They collect photos and videos, and have identified 459 individual cats from their distinctive rosette patterns. Combined with citizen scientist data, the images provide a “treasure” of information about jaguars and their social interactions, according to Valeria Boron, lead author of the study and senior program adviser for Latin America with WWF UK. Boron told Mongabay in a video call that most of what scientists previously knew about jaguars came from camera traps and genetic testing, which can’t accurately capture the full range of their interactions. Analyzing 13 years of data, the team found that the Pantanal jaguars were much more social than expected, with significant differences between males and females. The researchers recorded 167 instances of jaguar pairs interacting: nearly half involved two males, 31% involved a male and a female, and just 17% involved two females. Roughly a quarter of the interactions were aggressive, 36.5% were neutral — individuals resting or hunting…
items.t: In Brazil’s prey-rich Pantanal, jaguars reveal a surprisingly social side

items.title: US renews push to open Pacific marine protected area to fishing
items.summary: The U.S. government has published proposed rules to allow commercial fishing in an area more than double the size of California inside a Pacific marine reserve that encompasses a network of islands, atolls, seamounts and coral reef systems. The proposed rules, published Nov. 9 by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), or NOAA Fisheries, would lift fishing restrictions around Johnston Atoll, Wake Island, and Jarvis Island in the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument (PIH). Commercial fishing would be permitted between 50 and 200 nautical miles (93-185 kilometers) from these islands, while waters within 50 nmi would remain off-limits to protect species and habitats. The total affected area covers 1 million square kilometers (408,000 square miles). In its proposal, NOAA says the rules would support the “long-term sustainability of U.S. fisheries,” and align with previous directives from the Trump administration to increase fishing in the Pacific, including a presidential proclamation in April calling for the “unleashing” of commercial fishing in the PIH. At the same time, NOAA also says fishing in the PIH may only have a “minor” beneficial impact on fisheries operations and management. The proposed rules are open for public comment until Dec. 9. Activists have criticized the proposal and NOAA Fisheries’ characterization of the potential harm to cultural resources and protected species as “negligible.” “The ocean has always been a place of connection for Pacific peoples, and the Pacific Islands Heritage…
items.t: US renews push to open Pacific marine protected area to fishing

items.title: After years of speculation, Suriname evicts Mennonites farming in the Amazon
items.summary: More than 50 Mennonites have been deported from Suriname following years of controversy over plans to establish agricultural settlements for large-scale farming in the Amazon Rainforest. Authorities removed the Mennonites, members of a conservative Christian group that rejects modern technology, from state land in Suriname’s Sipaliwini district. They had been staying in the area with expired residency permits, according to a statement from the president’s office. On Oct. 31, they were reportedly flown to Bolivia, from where they originally came. “The point is essentially that the primary Amazon Rainforest is not being cut down for large-scale agriculture. I am opposed to that,” Suriname President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons told local media in an Oct. 4 interview, per a statement published by her office. In 2023 and 2024, Mongabay exposed plans to transfer hundreds of thousands of hectares of rainforest to Suriname’s Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (LVV). The plan involved relocating Mennonites from other areas in Latin America, including Belize and Bolivia, to Suriname to help develop large-scale farming projects that could boost the country’s domestic food production. Mennonites have a track record of rapid, profitable agribusiness development across the Americas — but often at the expense of forests. In some cases, their expansion has resulted in illegal deforestation. Roughly 93% of Suriname is covered in forest. Some of the Mennonite agriculture projects were cancelled following backlash over protecting the country’s forest cover and net-negative carbon…
items.t: After years of speculation, Suriname evicts Mennonites farming in the Amazon

items.title: Smallholder farmers struggle on El Niño frontline; will the world help?
items.summary: Smallholder farmers across the globe are bracing for, or already feeling, the effects of a historically strong El Niño. This event — forecast to peak in December with lasting impacts deep into 2027 — has brought warnings of shocks to global food prices and food security. The record-breaking 2026-2027 El Niño could drive an additional 49 million people into acute hunger, according to the United Nations, with southern Africa and Central America likely hardest hit. Expectations are that supplies of key staples such as rice and corn and commodities like cocoa, coffee and palm oil will be deeply reduced. Millions of smallholder farmers who grow the food we consume are on the frontline of these impacts, experts say. Palm oil suppliers in Indonesia, for example, are already reporting losses due to a prolonged El Niño-linked drought, while in Sudan long delayed rains are raising risk of widespread famine. In Central America, Guatemalan farmers are seeing sharp reductions in crops meant for home food consumption. The governments of El Salvador, Honduras and Panama have all issued El Niño emergency declarations, as have Bolivia and Peru in South America. “Fairtrade producers that we’re talking to are already seeing impacts,” Amanda Archila, CEO of Fairtrade America, told Mongabay in a video interview. “You’re already seeing clear signs of a dramatic increase in the number of food insecure smallholders.” Key cash crops could be far more deeply impacted over the coming months. The current El Niño is exposing a fundamental weakness in global food…This article was originally…
items.t: Smallholder farmers struggle on El Niño frontline; will the world help?

items.title: Canadian extractive firms displaced 300,000 in Africa since 1996, report says
items.summary: Canadian extractive industries have been linked to the displacement of at least 300,000 people in Africa over the past 30 years, the Justice and Corporate Accountability Project (JCAP) said in an October report. The York University-based group reviewed media reports, court documents and other sources to compile the 193-page report, which analyzed the Canadian government’s response to allegations of corruption and human rights abuses against 23 firms since 1996. The report said that Canadian officials repeatedly lent diplomatic support to companies accused of serious human rights abuses or lapses in worker safety. In 2017, for example, Canada’s High Commissioner to Tanzania met with the country’s Minister of Mines to advocate for Barrick Mining Corporation’s local subsidiary during a dispute over taxes and export policy, per the report. The meeting came just a year after a government inquiry heard reports that police guarding Barrick’s North Mara gold mine had killed dozens of people on its premises. “They always take the side of the company,” said report co-author Shin Imai, a professor at York University’s Osgoode Hall Law School, in an interview with Mongabay. “I have not seen an instance when they didn’t lobby [on their behalf].” In 2024, the advocacy group Human Rights Watch said that police guarding the North Mara mine were involved in a “growing number of unaccounted for killings.” The report’s annex included a 12-page response from Barrick that said it had been “targeted and criticized by irresponsible NGOs.” Canada’s enforcement of laws meant to prevent…
items.t: Canadian extractive firms displaced 300,000 in Africa since 1996, report says

items.title: Taiwan’s tea growers adapt to climate change by letting nature take control
items.summary: In the high-altitude Alishan mountain region of central Taiwan, tea growers cultivating prized oolong tea face mounting environmental crises: Between 2014 and 2023, local tea production dropped by 13.5% due to severe climate pressures and soil degradation. In response, a group of farmers is abandoning chemical inputs for nature-based solutions and wild cultivation, reports contributor Aylin Ho for Mongabay. Alishan has warmed by 0.7° Celsius (1.26° Fahrenheit) over the past decade, nearly triple Taiwan’s average rate. The hotter weather has caused mist to dissipate, which otherwise blocks sunlight and helps tea leaves stay moist. Warming has also intensified spring droughts. “Over the past five years, tea growers have experienced two or three spring droughts, at a time when they need water the most,” said Huang Cho-ying, chair of the Department of Geography at National Taiwan University in Taipei. Huang added that heavy winter rainfall and landslides further exacerbate crop damage. The use of chemical fertilizers over the years “has made the soil more acidic and has reduced the availability of certain nutrients to plants,” said Jiang Hong, an associate professor in the Department of Geography and Environment at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa. Lin Kuang-li, 60-year-old sixth-generation grower, transitioned away from pesticides to natural farming 30 years ago in Longyanlin village. Lin grows alfalfa to make “green manure,” and uses cut branches as ground cover to retain topsoil moisture. “My soil has a better capacity to absorb and drain water than soil treated with…
items.t: Taiwan’s tea growers adapt to climate change by letting nature take control

items.title: Communities around DRC’s Upemba National Park say conservation comes at a cost
items.summary: A forest can be many things to the communities that live in and around it. It can serve as farmland, a pharmacy, a food source or a cultural center. The forest can be a lifeline to residents who depend on it for survival. Yet access to that land can be restricted if it lies within a protected area. This is a common scenario in many parts of the world, where areas of high ecological value are also home to ecosystems that local communities depend on for survival. A growing body of research underscores the tensions that can arise when protected areas under conservation  overlap with community lands. One case in point is Kisandji, an ethnically diverse village in the southeastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo about 13 kilometers (8 miles) from Upemba National Park in Haut-Katanga province. The residents of Kisandji use the natural resources found in the park for food, medicine and farming. But since 2015, access to the parkland has become difficult for residents amid national efforts to combat poaching and wildlife crimes. The park’s territory has been a source of livelihood for surrounding communities, including in Kisandji, where around 85% of households depend primarily on farming. Without electricity, piped water or healthcare, Kisandji residents also depend heavily on nature for food, medicine and income. Additionally, in a landscape shaped by war, displacement, poverty, mining and other extractive activities that interfere with people’s subsistence activities and lives, the forests within the park remain their go-to source…This article was originally…
items.t: Communities around DRC’s Upemba National Park say conservation comes at a cost

Nature has a way of coming up with some truly extraordinary creatures, and sometimes, the real world looks more imaginative than fiction. From animals with bizarre body shapes and unusual patterns to creatures with features that seem almost impossible, the natural world is full of surprises. Some look like they belong in a fantasy movie, while others could easily be mistaken for characters from an animated film. 

In fact, scientists have identified more than 1.5 million animal species, and researchers believe millions more may still be undiscovered. With such incredible diversity, it's hardly surprising that some creatures look like they were invented rather than found in nature. 

A Threads discussion recently invited people to share photos of the most made-up-looking animals they had ever seen. items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.
items.t: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.
items.t: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

items.title: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry
items.summary:
Proponents argue ocean carbon removal is necessary to counteract the effects of the climate crisis but critics say more research is needed

A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.

“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.

Continue reading...
items.t: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry

items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.
items.t: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

items.title: Vietnam’s freshwater obsession leaves decades-long scars for Mekong Delta farmers
items.summary: BÌNH ĐẠI, Vietnam — For centuries, the Mekong River emptied into the South China Sea through nine vast estuaries, earning it the name Cửu Long, Vietnamese for “Nine Dragons.” In the 1960s, natural deposition of sand swallowed the first dragon, the Bassac River. Now, human-made infrastructure is choking the second, the Ba Lai River. More than two decades after a sluice gate began operating near the mouth of the Ba Lai River in southern Vietnam, the river has turned into a stagnant lake, trapping pollutants and accelerating coastal erosion. Intended to protect the region from salinity, the megastructure has created problems and triggered conflicts between local farmers and authorities, sparking semi-open resistance that further destabilizes this already climate-vulnerable area. On a cloudy day in September, Nguyên, a shrimp farmer in Bình Đại commune in Vĩnh Long province, calculates when he should harvest his shrimp as he prepares to feed his two ponds. During the rainy season, water pollution is his primary concern, and a miscalculation can wipe out his entire stock. “This month, the sluice discharges water on the eighth, ninth, 21st, and 22nd, so I will harvest my shrimp on the fifth or sixth,” says Nguyên, which is not his real name. He asks to use a pseudonym due to the sensitive nature of the issue. “Fruit farmers in the freshwater zone use tons of pesticides and herbicides,” Nguyên tells Mongabay. “The chemicals linger on the ground. When it rains, the runoff flows into canals and the river, heavily contaminating…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Vietnam’s freshwater obsession leaves decades-long scars for Mekong Delta farmers

items.title: Wildlife trade regulator CITES lifts sanctions against Laos, prompting conservation concerns
items.summary: CHIANG MAI, Thailand — Global wildlife trade regulator CITES has lifted trade sanctions against Laos, opening the door for the Southeast Asian nation to resume trade of long-tailed macaques and other species. Some conservationists called the move “premature,” arguing that Laos must do more to curb the illegal wildlife trade, which is estimated to be worth billions of dollars a year globally. Laos was sanctioned in 2023 for its failure to rein in criminal networks trading illegal wildlife products with near-impunity and to regulate bear bile and tiger farms. But the country has made “significant progress” in addressing these issues, CITES’ Standing Committee said in Geneva on Nov. 4. While Laos will now be able to trade in CITES-listed animals without special restriction, it does not end the review process for Laos. Ongoing monitoring of Laos’ adherence to CITES rules will determine its ability to continue exporting species listed under the convention. A mousedeer, most likely Tragulus williamsoni, and silver pheasants for sale in the morning market at Luang Namtha in northern Laos. Image courtesy of William Bleisch. “We recognize that sustained progress requires continued investigations, prosecutions, demand reduction and effective oversight of wildlife facilities,” Somvang Phimmavong, director-general of Laos’ Department of Forestry, wrote in an email to Mongabay. In 2025, a joint Mongabay investigation with NGO GI-TOC identified 35 illegal wildlife shopping sites in Vientiane and Luang Prabang selling ivory, rhino horn, pangolin scales and other illegal wildlife products…
items.t: Wildlife trade regulator CITES lifts sanctions against Laos, prompting conservation concerns

items.title: Coyote officials thought they had killed after child attack seen alive in LA neighborhood
items.summary:
Animal that menaced residents was shot in October but then reappeared – and was shot for a second time and killed

A coyote that California wildlife officials believed they had euthanized after it bit a toddler and menaced residential pets in a trendy Los Angeles neighborhood was seen alive recently, neighborhood residents said.

Wiley, the name some Atwater Village residents gave to the coyote, had vexed the area with its increasingly aggressive and brazen behavior. The wild animal, which scampered through people’s backyards, was reportedly being fed by an unidentified man. Wiley’s presence drew local uproar after he bit a 16-month-old child.

items.t: Coyote officials thought they had killed after child attack seen alive in LA neighborhood

items.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
items.summary:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.

Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

Continue reading...
items.t: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems

items.title: To boost conservation of kelp forests, start by naming them (commentary)
items.summary: Beneath the coppery fronds of the only floating bamboo kelp forest in the world, a creature shapeshifts across the reef. A tuberculate cuttlefish (Sepia tuberculata) has just escaped a predator using “pseudomorph-ink” — a ‘false body’ strategy of emitting ink clouds that resemble its shape — while the actual animal jets away in the opposite direction. Once hidden under a rock or in a crevice, its superb camouflage and mimicry will protect it from detection. This animal lives in the Great African Seaforest, which stretches for more than 1,300 kilometers (just over 800 miles) from South Africa to Namibia. This ecosystem is just one of many such kelp forests across the world that together house thousands of kinds of creatures all hiding, breeding, sheltering and feeding. However, their homes are in trouble. Proponents say kelp forests like the Great African Seaforest deserve the same attention that other marine ecosystems like coral reefs and mangrove forests receive. Image courtesy of Jannes Landschoff / Sea Change Project. Fringing a third of the world’s coastlines in temperate and polar waters, kelp forests are one of the most biodiverse nearshore ecosystems on our planet and are probably as biologically important as rainforests. Despite this, less than 2% of them are meaningfully protected and warming water could wipe out up to 25 million hectares (almost 62 million acres) of kelp forests by 2050. Then, this August, the global ocean surface hit its highest temperature on record. Kelp forests are biodiversity powerhouses that provide valuable ecosystem…This article…
items.t: To boost conservation of kelp forests, start by naming them (commentary)

items.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.
items.t: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought

items.title: This ocean liner was the world’s fastest. It’s being sunk to make the largest artificial reef
items.summary: DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — An ocean liner that once was the fastest on the seas is headed to its final home on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico as the world’s largest artificial reef. Officials on Florida’s panhandle coast were scuttling the SS United States on Wednesday about 25 miles southwest of Destin, between Panama City and Pensacola. The $13.5 million project is designed to attract more divers and fishing enthusiasts to the area while creating a home for tuna, marlin and swordfish. The project will keep what had been a technological marvel from becoming scrap metal. The 990-foot ship set a speed record on its first voyage in 1952. By John Hanna and Stephen Smith, Associated Press Banner image: The SS United States is towed down the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, from Philadelphia, Wednesday, Feb. 19, 2025. Image courtesy of Matt Rourke, Associated Press This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: This ocean liner was the world’s fastest. It’s being sunk to make the largest artificial reef

items.title: ‘Developed nations are not honoring their commitments’: DRC negotiator on biodiversity finance
items.summary: YEREVAN, Armenia — Discussions were running much longer — and tenser — than they were supposed to during one of the last sessions of the 2026 U.N. biodiversity summit (COP17) in Armenia. The recurring culprit: Money, or more specifically, biodiversity finance. It recalled earlier discussions four years ago during the COP15 summit in Montreal, which ended in momentary panic when one party threatened to pull out at the last minute over finance issues. One of the parties at the center of disagreements during both summits was the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC): Holder of the biggest share of the second-largest rainforest in the world — the Congo Basin — and fierce critic on the world stage for increased, and “more effective,” finance to help industrially developing countries meet global biodiversity goals. Among the recurring figures representing the country at environmental conferences is Daniel Mukubi, often on the microphone, intervening and vocal about better and more equitable access to finance. “All this weight … the objectives, targets of the global biodiversity framework … It requires additional efforts for developing countries, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, to be able to find alternatives,” says Mukubi in an exclusive interview with Mongabay. “Additional means to enable Indigenous peoples and local communities that depend on forests and ecosystems, but also on forest products for their livelihoods, to be able to find means of subsistence that will allow them not to continue destroying the forest.” A local person carrying firewood, Yangambi, Tshopo,…
items.t: ‘Developed nations are not honoring their commitments’: DRC negotiator on biodiversity finance

items.title: Genetic study describes two new species of Amazonian howler monkeys
items.summary: A sweeping genetic study of howler monkeys has revealed two previously unrecognized species in the Amazon, identified a potentially distinct species in the Caribbean and prompted researchers to reconsider how several populations are classified. The new study examined genetic relationships across the genus Alouatta, using genomic data, physical characteristics and museum specimens. Researchers formally described two Amazonian red howler monkeys: the Pantepui red howler monkey (Alouatta iroi) in northwestern Amazonia and the Mato Grosso red howler monkey (Alouatta matogrossensis) in the southern Brazilian Amazon. The research builds on more than a decade of fieldwork and sample collection. Lead author Romina Batista, a biologist at the University of Salford (UK) and Brazil’s National Institute of Amazonian Research, analyzed more than 2 terabytes of raw genomic data. The scale of the dataset helped reveal evolutionary differences that earlier studies had missed. While examining the results, Batista noticed that monkeys on opposite sides of the Branco River in northern Brazil formed distinct genetic lineages. Physical differences, including the more yellowish fur of A. iroi, supported the findings. “When I saw that, I literally called Jean and I said, ‘Jean, there is something different here,’” Batista said, referring to co-author Jean Boubli. Historical museum specimens also helped researchers identify characteristics distinguishing the populations. Batista said the findings demonstrate the importance of preserving natural history collections, which allowed the scientists to…
items.t: Genetic study describes two new species of Amazonian howler monkeys

items.title: Dock leaves: a handy but not very good cure for nettle stings | Brief letters
items.summary:
Sting relief | Romans in Scotland | A wild translation | Wrapping paper solution

I agree that dock leaves probably have no special properties for curing nettle stings (It is true that…, 9 November), but this raises the question of why our ancestors chose them. Two reasons are likely – first, dock leaves are easy for a non-specialist to identify, and second, docks are common plants with similar habitat preferences to the stinging nettle, which means they can usually be found nearby. There are many British plants that are probably more effective for nettle stings, but these are no help if the stung person cannot find them.
Dr Richard Milne
Senior lecturer in plant evolutionary biology, University of Edinburgh

• Any discussion of the Romans in Scotland (What did the Romans ever give Scotland? Heated floors, flashy sandals, sun gods – and a lot of nails, 5 November) should include the immortal words put into the mouth of the Caledonian chieftain Calgacus (the first named “Scot”) by the historian Tacitus after the Roman armies had ravaged the Highlands: “Ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant” (They make a desert and call it peace).
Harry D Watson
Edinburgh
items.t: Dock leaves: a handy but not very good cure for nettle stings | Brief letters

items.title: How would the Amazon react if it dried up? A 25-year-old field study has the answer
items.summary: A question hangs in the air while the soil of the planet’s largest tropical rainforest grows increasingly dry: What is the Amazon’s future facing extreme droughts in a warming world? To try to predict the fate of the biome, an ambitious experiment subjected an area of Amazon vegetation in Pará in northern Brazil to severe water stress for two decades. The findings reveal a surprising reshuffle of how the forest survives. The Esecaflor Project (Forest Drought Study Project) is the longest-running and most extensive scientific investigation of its kind ever conducted in a tropical forest. It has been underway for 25 years, during which its creators have sought to understand how the Amazon might respond to a prolonged lack of water in the soil. The experimental drought began in 2001. Covering a one-hectare (2.5-acre) area within the roughly 318,000 hectares (786,000 acres) of Caxiuanã National Forest in Pará, the project installed 6,000 transparent, rectangular plastic panels beneath the tree canopy, between 1 and 4 meters (3.3 and 13 feet) above the ground, to divert about 50% of rainwater away through gutters and channels. An undisturbed plot of equal size serves as a comparison area. In both forest plots, researchers monitor soil moisture, air temperature, tree growth, sap flow and root development, while two 40-m-(131-ft-)tall towers equipped with NASA radar transmit data to the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the U.S. state of California for processing. Plastic panels installed beneath the canopy in the Esecaflor Project study area divert rainwater to…This…
items.t: How would the Amazon react if it dried up? A 25-year-old field study has the answer

items.title: This Woman Adopted The Black Cat Of Her Dreams, And Watched Him Transform Into Something Extraordinary
items.summary:
When Brazilian photographer Kauane Stephanie adopted a little black kitten, she thought she’d finally found the pet she’d always dreamed of. What she couldn’t have imagined was that, just over a year later, her beloved feline would look almost completely different.

On June 12, 2024, Kauane, who lives in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, welcomed an adorable black kitten into her home as a birthday present. She named him Fumaça, which means “Smoke” in Portuguese. Having always wanted a black cat, she was delighted with her new companion, and the two quickly became inseparable. For the first year, Fumaça looked just like any other black cat. But then, Kauane noticed something strange. A tiny pink spot had appeared on his previously dark nose. At first, it didn’t seem particularly concerning, but over time, more changes appeared, including patches of his black fur gradually turning white.

Scroll down to read the rest of Fumaça’s story, and learn more about the condition that causes it.

items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.
items.t: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

items.title: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?
items.summary:
As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard

It began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1).

By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?

items.title: Humble house sparrows roosting in Spain evoke a childhood memory
items.summary:
Forget the hoopoes and the ring-necked parakeets, the highlight of our trip was a sound I hadn’t heard for 50 years

As dusk falls on a warm October evening, I gradually become aware of a strange, high-pitched sizzling noise. From our table outside a busy bar, with Spaniards celebrating their national holiday, it reminds me of water carelessly tossed into a scorching frying pan.

I approach a bougainvillea bush decked with rich purple flowers, and the collective clamour separates into distinct notes. I realise I am listening to hundreds – perhaps thousands – of house sparrows, each bird calling frantically to their companions as they gather to roost for the night. It’s a sound I haven’t heard for more than 50 years.

Continue reading...
items.t: Humble house sparrows roosting in Spain evoke a childhood memory

items.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
items.summary: A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.
items.t: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't

items.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.
items.t: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago

items.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
items.summary: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.
items.t: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

items.title: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction
items.summary:
Director Vincent Munier takes his father and son into the Vosges forest in France and finds lynx, serene foxes and deer

Cannily timed to overlap but also contrast with the BBC’s Blue Planet III, this French nature documentary embodies a very different way to go about things. Instead of the detached, friendly style of David Attenborough with his generous sprinkle of zoological facts and figures, Whispers in the Woods is a more emotionally driven, visually stylised work that emphasises the interaction of the human and the animal realm.

Its director, Vincent Munier, previously made The Velvet Queen, a swooning study of his and writer Sylvain Tesson’s search for snow leopards in Tibet. This time round, Munier places his father Michel, a naturalist, and his own teenage son Simon at the centre of the action; we experience the film largely through Simon’s bright eyes as Michel teaches him about the ecosystem in the Vosges forest in eastern France. The result is a subtle, tender work that evokes the need to pass on interest and engagement in the natural world to younger generations, but which manages to avoid feeling too preachy or sanctimonious. It helps that the soundtrack, composed by Nick Cave’s key collaborator Warren Ellis, consistently evokes a wistful sense of awe with its sighing strings and keening voices, all of which meshes beautifully with the soundscape of the beasties we see here. (It isn’t called Whispers in the Woods for…
items.t: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction

items.title: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkably preserved 450-million-year-old fossil containing soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative, revealing unexpected details about marine life more than 200 million years before dinosaurs existed. Found in a museum collection, the extraordinarily rare specimen offers new clues about how Earth's earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved.
items.t: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

items.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the wattle bird who dive-bombed me
items.summary:
To help native birds through the winter, I put out honey. It worked a treat until one chased the rest off – and then turned on me

The error took place last autumn when I offered honey to the nectar feeding birds in my neighbourhood in a bay-side suburb of Melbourne. Our grevilleas, which would normally attract them, hadn’t flowered, and my stopgap would hopefully see Australia’s native birds through the winter. With luck, magpies, pardalotes and ravens would discourage intrusion by an increasing population of common mynas – notorious for their aggressive displacement of native species.

It worked, at first. Wattle birds visited in greater numbers. One, whom we named Wally, aggressively saw off the mynas. He arrived wan and thin, and I watched him grow plump and hale.

items.title: Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets
items.summary:
Established in UK cities for decades and much loved for their green plumage, the Himalayan birds have been recast as an ecological threat. But is the idea of invasive species itself a problem?

Before we saw a single parakeet, we heard them: a disembodied static that grew louder as we approached Hither Green cemetery in south-east London. It was an early evening in late June, and we had come to witness an invasion. By the time my friend and I reached the cemetery’s western edge, the clamour was all-encompassing. We hopped the fence and picked our way through the gravestones. Above us now were the birds themselves, their kryptonite-green plumage, scab-red beaks, pearly black collars and trailing tail feathers unmistakable: Psittacula krameri, the ring-necked parakeet.

Hither Green cemetery hosts one of the city’s largest roosts. Every day at dusk, a sizeable chunk of London’s feral parakeet population returns here, to a specific line of poplars. They like to spend the night in the company of their own kind. We watched them come first in ones and twos, and then in larger chirrupping squadrons. Hundreds of them, and then thousands. At maximum capacity, the trees fizzed. Here was a pandemonium, a parakeet concourse. It gave the impression of community, greeting and conversation. “This,” my friend said, “would make a great cheap first date.”

items.t: Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets

items.title: Auckland hit by swarms of bees after milder than usual New Zealand winter
items.summary:
Beekeepers say they are fielding a record number of calls from people needing assistance in removing swarms

Engulfing parked cars and blanketing inner-city street signs – New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland, is in the midst of an unusually large bee swarming season, that experts say has been exacerbated by a milder than usual winter.

The Auckland Beekeepers Club says it is fielding five to 10 calls a day, requesting assistance to remove swarms of bees – with individual members of the club being contacted for help as well.

items.summary:

  • Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

With just 13 animals left, time was running out for the Leadbeater’s possums at Yellingbo conservation area.

The critically endangered forest sprites have exacting habitat needs. They prefer cool, wet and dark forest, with large old trees to nest in and a dense thicket of paperbarks and tea trees to dart and hide in.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
items.summary: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

items.title: 40 Tiny Puppies Snuggled Up To Their Parents That Might Melt Your Heart, As Shared By This Page
items.summary:
Few things can compete with a puppy curled up against a parent ten times its size. The little one is all round belly, velvet ears, and paws that seem borrowed from a much bigger animal, while the grown-up lies perfectly still so the nap won’t be disturbed. Put the two side by side and the cuteness doubles: same coat, same eyes, same slightly puzzled expression, only in a pocket-sized edition.

That’s the charm of this collection from the Facebook page Rocadog, which gathers some of its sweetest shots of puppies with their mothers and fathers. Some of the youngsters copy their parent’s pose so faithfully it looks rehearsed. Others have given up on posing altogether and are snoozing on a furry back, while a few stare into the camera with eyes so big and round they barely seem real.

items.title: This grim story of marine park whales could yet have a positive outcome – if it teaches us to value other species | Elle Hunt
items.summary:
There is no ‘saving’ these traumatised mammals from places like Marineland in Canada. Humans need to understand that our actions are not easily undone

Remember “Save the whales”? Now that was an environmental campaign everyone could get behind. Surely you don’t want whales to die!

It may have got the 1986 global ban on commercial whaling over the line, but in these sophisticated times that slogan seems woefully reductive, even naive. As Greenpeace warns on its website, 40 years later: “There is still more work to be done to save the whales.” Yes. You might say, surveying the state of our ocean ecosystems, there’s quite a bit.

Elle Hunt is a freelance journalist

items.title: A new start after 60: I was burnt out and facing redundancy. So I set up a bee farm – and learned the joys of a simple life
items.summary:
Jeff Lee had spent decades as an investigative journalist. But when he upped sticks with his wife to buy a farm in rural British Columbia, he didn’t just change jobs – he found a different way to live

Jeff Lee became interested in beekeeping in his late 50s after his wife, Amanda, took part in a “beard of bees” event at Science World’s “science of fear” exhibition in Vancouver, Canada, where they lived. She stepped into a Perspex booth, a caged queen bee was placed beneath her chin and thousands of bees climbed her neck – hence the “beard”. She was so calm that the stallholder was impressed. “You should keep bees,” he said.

Lee had a small collection of books on the insects – “the idea of homesteading and having something of an independent life, rather than a rat-race life, always appealed to me” – and the pair enrolled on a beekeeping course. Before long, they had put two hives in their back yard. Fast-forward to 60 and he and Amanda had moved 300 miles east to rural British Columbia to buy a bee farm. For Lee’s part, however, he didn’t just acquire a business. The bees taught him a completely different way to live.

items.title: Country diary: Teasing out spiders with a tuning fork | Susie White
items.summary:
Hexham, Northumberland: Revelations aplenty as we embark on a spider hunt with a man called Fran who knows his arachnids

We gathered at the bandstand, an elegant Edwardian building in the abbey grounds, all slender ironwork and tented top. Fran Garcia was leading a spider walk and our group of 10 included two children, one of them my granddaughter. Fran is a member of the British Arachnological Society and communicates knowledge with lively humour.

As an introduction to spiders he explained their anatomy and web building using a bizarre range of items: wire and ropes of varying thicknesses, a bottle of glue, a folding knife to demonstrate tarantula jaws. Then Fran passed around an egg sac from a wasp spider, Argiope bruennichi, a species found in southern England but moving north. Teardrop-shaped and papery, it was subtly marked in grey and beige to blend with grasses.
